title: I’ve been fined over my crypto and want to appeal
excerpt: The penalty is defended separately from the tax assessment. What can be challenged, what the deadlines are and why, with crypto assets, a reasonable interpretation of the law is a real argument.

hero.h1: Accepting the assessment doesn’t mean you have to accept the penalty
hero.subheading: They are two separate proceedings and are defended separately. The tax itself may be correctly calculated and the penalty may still not stand, because a penalty requires more than having under-declared.

sections.body:
You’ve received a tax assessment — what the tax authorities calculate you should have paid — and, together with it or afterwards, notice that penalty proceedings have been opened. It may stem from an information request you answered yourself, from a limited review or from a tax inspection.

The first thing to understand is that they are not the same. The assessment corrects the tax due. The penalty punishes conduct, and to impose it the tax authorities must give reasoned grounds for culpability — that there was fault, even if only simple negligence. Establishing that you under-declared is not enough.

With crypto assets that point is especially open to challenge, and not as a matter of rhetoric: for years much of the activity — swaps, staking, airdrops, DeFi — had no clear, published administrative guidance.

sections.entrada: They can be combined: in some cases it makes sense to accept the tax due and contest only the penalty.

items: Corrects the tax due for the year
Is argued with figures: rebuilding your transactions and showing where every euro came from
If the tax authorities started from incomplete data, that is where the defence lies
Accepting it may reduce the penalty, which is worth weighing up beforehand
Requires the tax authorities to give reasons for culpability, even if only negligence
Is challenged with a reasonable interpretation of the law and the absence of concealment
Follows its own proceedings, with its own deadlines

sections.entrada: The exact dates depend on your notification. This is the usual sequence.

hitos.body: Every deadline runs from here. Note the date of notification, not the date you read it.
The notification itself states the time allowed. It’s the cheapest point at which to defend yourself, because there is no final decision yet.

hitos.titulo: Appeal for reconsideration (recurso de reposición) or economic-administrative claim
hitos.body: Once the decision has been notified, the general deadline for appealing through the administrative route is one month. Reconsideration and the economic-administrative claim are alternatives, and you have to choose one.
If no appeal is filed in time, the penalty becomes final and the remaining options narrow considerably.

sections.h2: What can be argued against a crypto penalty
bullets: Reasonable interpretation of the law: if the administrative position had not been published, or was contradictory, when the return was filed, the conduct cannot be penalised simply because it doesn’t match the current position.
No concealment: you traded on platforms that report, moved funds through your bank and didn’t use opaque structures. That carries weight.
Failure to give reasons for culpability: penalty decisions that merely describe the outcome without reasoning about the conduct can be challenged on that ground.
Material error in the base: if the assessment treats internal movements between your own wallets as sales, the base for the penalty was miscalculated from the outset.
Evidence of due diligence: having taken professional advice, having asked for information or having declared other years correctly are facts that can be put forward.
Proportionality and grading: a review of the criteria applied to grade the penalty and of whether the circumstances the tax authorities relied on are actually present.

steps.title: We separate what is being disputed
steps.body: We check whether the tax due is correctly calculated and whether the penalty is properly reasoned. They are different analyses and can lead to different decisions.

steps.title: We rebuild the base
steps.body: If the assessment starts from incomplete data, that is shown with your reworked transactions. Many penalties fall because the base they are calculated on is inflated.

steps.title: We choose the route
steps.body: Reconsideration or economic-administrative claim, depending on the amount, the subject matter and the strategy. They are mutually exclusive, so choosing wrongly closes doors.

steps.title: We draft and file within the deadline
steps.body: With the documentary and on-chain evidence to support each argument, and explaining to you beforehand what holds up and on what basis.

steps.title: We follow it through to the decision
steps.body: And, with the decision in front of us, we assess with you whether it’s worth going further.

items.q: Is it worth appealing, or will it cost me more?
items.a: It depends on the amount and the grounds, and that’s exactly what we analyse before recommending anything. In some cases the cost of the procedure isn’t justified by the amount at stake, and we’ll tell you so. We don’t appeal for the sake of it.

items.q: Can I accept the assessment and appeal only the penalty?
items.a: Yes, and with crypto assets it’s a common strategy: the tax due may be correctly calculated while the penalty isn’t properly reasoned. That said, agreeing to the assessment can affect the reductions available on the penalty, so the decision is made with both figures in front of you.

Suspension of enforcement isn’t automatic and usually requires a guarantee, although penalties are subject to their own specific rules. It’s one of the first things to settle, because it affects your cash flow while the procedure lasts.

items.q: What if I’ve already missed the deadline?
items.a: The options narrow considerably, but they don’t always disappear: there are special review procedures with strict requirements. It’s worth looking into, though it’s best not to count on it.

items.q: Can you guarantee the penalty will be cancelled?
items.a: No, and be wary of anyone who guarantees it. We don’t publish success rates or predict how a decision will go. What we do is build the best documented position possible and tell you frankly how we see it.

cierre.body: Tell us exactly what you’ve received and on what date it was notified to you. With that we know what deadline you have, whether to make submissions or appeal, and which part of the case is worth pursuing.
